label: text
content: Considering DNA sequencing data (whole-genome sequencing or exome sequencing), referenced-based assembly often follows the goal of finding the differences between an individual's genome and the reference genome for the corresponding species, rather than characterizing the genome of that species in the first place

label: text

label: text

label: text

label: text
content: - Identification of DNA binding by transcription factors (ChIP-seq)

label: text

label: paragraph_title

label: text

label: text

label: text

label: text
content: - Computational identification of high-quality mutations from sequencing data

label: text
content: - Requirement: reads must be aligned/mapped to the reference genome

label: text
content: - We will use this as a motivation to align/map reads to the reference genome, but:

label: text
content: As already mentioned: read alignment / read mapping / reference-based assembly is useful also for purposes other than variant calling!

label: paragraph_title
content: A standard clinical test for personalized medicine?

label: text
content: - Precision medicine: stratification of patients based on large-scale data (e.g., DNA-seq), beyond classical "signs-and-symptoms approach (König et al, 2017)

label: text
content: - Personalized medicine: tailoring of medical treatment to the individual characteristics (e.g., genetic profile) of each patient; e.g., by predicting which medical treatments will be safe and effective for a patient (Cirillo & Valencia, 2019

label: text
content: - Genome (or exome) sequencing can be extremely useful for (some) patients with rare genetic diseases or cancer

label: text
content: - It is still not very useful for common genetic diseases (usually complex diseases with small contributions by individual mutations)

label: text
content: - But: Clinical NGS sequencing is rapidly gaining in importance in many areas

label: paragraph_title
content: So why not use de novo assembly?

label: text
content: - De novo assembly algorithms with de Bruijn graphs are computational demanding and error-prone

label: text

label: text

label: text

label: paragraph_title
content: Tries

label: text
content: A trie (from retrieval), is a multi-way tree structure useful for storing strings over an alphabet

label: text
content: banana$

label: text
content: - Usually pronounced like "try"

label: text
content: bandana$

label: text
content: - A data structure for representing a collection of strings

label: text
content: - Fast pattern matching within this collection

label: vision_footnote
content: Let's make a trie for this collection of "reads"

label: text
content: A trie is defined formally as the smallest tree over an alphabet $ \Sigma $ such that

label: text
content: - Each edge of the trie is labeled with one character $ c \in \Sigma$

label: text
content: - A node has at most one outgoing edge labeled for each $ c \in \Sigma$ (i.e., at most $ |\Sigma$ outgoing edges)

label: text
content: - Each key (string contained in the trie) is "spelled out" along some path starting at the root (i.e., one-to-one correspondence to a path from the root to a leaf!)

label: text
content: Tries can be constructed to have all of the suffixes of some larger string be the keys

label: paragraph_title
content: Trie: that pesky dollar sign

label: text
content: $ is a symbol that does not appear anywhere else in our genome template $ T (i.e., not part of our alphabet $ \Sigma)

label: text
content: - We define it to be lexicographically "less" than our other characters

label: text
content: - For instance, for nucleotide sequences we would have $ < A < C < G < T

label: text
content: - The $ enforces a lexicographic rule that we know from dictionaries: For instance, "over" comes before "overture"

label: text
content: - For instance, AC comes before AC because we are actually comparing AC$ with ACG and by definition $AC$

label: text
content: - $ also ensures that no suffix will be considered as a prefix of any other suffix (e.g., "an" would be prefix of an"anna$" is not a prefix of any other suffix

label: text
content: This is important to make sure that each key or word in the trie has a one-to-one correspondence with one specific path from the root to a leaf!

label: text
content: - Example: the trie of the previous slide does not contain the individual word "an", because we don't have a path from root to leaf for that word; we'd need a path "root $ \rightarrow a n \rightarrow$ "$!$"

label: paragraph_title
content: Trie

label: text
content: - So what have we gained?

label: text
content: - Recall the running time of the simple naive algorithm was $ \mathcal{O}(G\cdot n_b)$ with

label: text
content: $ \triangleright G $ being the genome length and

label: text
content: $ n_{b}=\ell \cdot L $ being the combined length of reads (total sequenced bases) and $ L $ the average read length

label: text
content: - If $ L^{\prime} $ L^{\prime} $ is the maximum length of any read, then the runtime of the trie algorithm is the $ \mathcal{O}(L^{\prime}\cdot G)$ for matching and $ n_{b}$

label: text
content: But ... the amount of memory required for the trie is in the worst case proportional to the total length of the reads, which can be enormous: $ \mathcal{O}(n_b)$

label: text
content: Can we flip the paradigm and preprocess the genome?

label: paragraph_title
content: Trie

label: text
content: In the previous example, we made a trie out of the "reads" and slid this trie across our "genome" to search for matches. Let us now examine another strategy that will take us to suffix trees and suffix arrays

label: paragraph_title
content: Trie T: MISSISSIPPI

label: paragraph_title
content: T$: MISSISSIPPI$

label: text
content: Instead of using different words for the trie, let's use all suffixes of $T$!$

label: text
content: - Hence, each path from the root to a leaf represents a suffix, and each suffix is represented by a path from the root to a leaf (including the full string and the empty suffix "$"!

label: text
content: - The nodes have implicit labels that reflect the string of characters on the path from the root to the node

label: paragraph_title
content: Trie

label: text
content:
MISS is a substring of $T$
$MIST is not a substring of $T$

label: text
content: - Each substring of $ T $ is represented by a path from the root, i.e., every substring is a prefix of some suffix of $ T $

label: text
content: - Thus to search for a substring S, start at the root and follow the edges labeled with the characters of S

label: text
content: - If at some point there is no outgoing edge for the next character of S, then S is not a substring of T

label: paragraph_title
content: Trie

label: text
content: PI is a substring of $ T $

label: text
content: PI is also a suffix of $ T $

label: text
content: - A string S is a suffix of T if it is a substring and the final node on the walk has an outgoing edge labeled $

label: paragraph_title
content: Trie

label: text
content: The substring SI occurs twice in $ T!$

label: text
content: How often does "I" occur in T?

label: text
content: - How many times does some substring $ S $ occur in $ T? $

label: text
content: - Follow the path for S

label: text
content: - If we finish at some node n, then S occurs the same number of times as the number of leaf nodes in the subtree rooted at n

label: text
content: - Another reason why suffixes need a terminal "$"; e.g., check occurrences of "i" in $T$

label: paragraph_title
content: Trie

label: text
content: ISSI is the longest repeated substring

label: text
content: - What is the longest repeated substring S of T?

label: text
content: This is the depth of the deepest node with 2 or more children!

label: paragraph_title
content: Suffix trie: size complexity

label: text
content: We would like to know the limits for the size of a suffix trie

label: text
content: - How many nodes does a suffix trie have if the string it is based on has $ m = | T|$ characters?

label: text
content: - Simplest case: a string of minimum complexity (repetition of the same character)

label: text
content: Consider the string $ T = aaaa$ , i.e., m "a"s in a row

label: text
content: There is one root

label: text
content: There are m nodes with an incoming "a" edge

label: text
content: There are m+1 nodes with an incoming "$" edge

label: text
content: Total 2m+2 nodes, i.e., $ \mathcal{O}(m)$ nodes

label: paragraph_title
content: Suffix trie: size complexity

label: text
content: We would like to know the limits for the size of a suffix trie

label: text
content: - How many nodes does a suffix trie have if the string it is based on has $ m = | T|$ characters?

label: text
content: - Consider the string $ T = AAABBB$ with $n=3$ "A"s, n=3 "$ "B"$ and $m=2n$

label: text
content: There is one root

label: text
content: There are n nodes on the "B" chain (right)

label: text
content: There are n nodes on the "A" chain (middle)

label: text
content: There are n chains having n "B" nodes (hanging from each "A" node)

label: text
content: There are 2n+1 "$" nodes (not shown here; one for each suffix, including the empty suffix)

label: text
content: Total $ n^{2}+4n+2$ nodes, i.e., $ \mathcal{O}\left(n^{2}\right)$ nodes

label: figure_title
content: ($ omitted for better readability)

label: paragraph_title
content: Suffix trie: size complexity

label: text
content: - Thus, we have seen two example string classes with size complexity (number of nodes that grow at $ \mathcal{O}(m^{2})$

label: text
content: - The above figure shows that the worst case is $ \mathcal{O} ( m^{2} $

label: text
content: Height: length of longest suffix (=original string!) + 1 (for the $) = m+1

label: text
content: Maximum width: maximum number of leaf nodes (= number of suffixes!) = m

label: text
content: - On real life data, the number of nodes grows more than linearly but less than quadratically - still usually too much to be practical ...

label: text
content: Remember: human genome has >3 billion "letters"

label: paragraph_title
content: Suffix trie: size complexity

label: text
content: The challenge of algorithmic development for NGS read aligners/mappers is basically to make string indices smaller and faster. We will go through various ideas that take us from the suffix trie to the suffix tree ...

label: text
content: - Combine non-branching paths into a single edge with a string label

label: text
content: - Replace the string label with $ \mathcal{O}(1)$ references to the original "genome" string

label: text
content: - $ \mathcal{O}(n)$ "online" method for constructing suffix tree (Ukkonen, 1995)

label: paragraph_title
content: From suffix trie to suffix tree

label: text
content: - Combine non-branching paths into a single edge with a string label

label: text
content: - This clearly reduces the number of nodes and edges

label: text
content: - As a side effect, it ensures that all internal nodes have more than one child node

label: paragraph_title
content: From suffix trie to suffix tree

label: text
content: - Example: $ T=MISSISSIPPI$

label: text
content: $ m=\operatorname{length}(T)=1 2$ (including the termination character $) $

label: text
content: - Once non-branching paths are combined into single edges, what is the effect on the number of leaves and internal nodes?

label: paragraph_title
content: From suffix trie to suffix tree

label: text
content: - We have the root node and m leaf nodes (obvious, since we have m suffixes)

label: text
content: - What can we say about the number of internal nodes?

label: text
content: If a full binary tree has m leaf nodes, it has exactly $ m-1$ internal nodes

label: text
content: Our tree has at most as many internal nodes as a full binary tree If an internal node has > 2 children then we have fewer parent nodes!

label: text
content: - Thus, there are $ \leq 2m$ total nodes, i.e., $ \mathcal{O}(m)$ nodes

label: text
content: $ m $ [suffixes] + 1 [root] + ( \leq m - 1 ] [internal nodes] $

label: text
content: - Edges? Each leaf and internal node has one incoming edge, so $ \leq 2 m - 1!

label: paragraph_title
content: From suffix trie to suffix tree

label: text
content: - Thus, the number of nodes is now linear in the size of the input

label: text
content: - BUT: the total length of the edge labels is still $ \mathcal{O}\left(m^{2}$

label: paragraph_title
content: From suffix trie to suffix tree

label: paragraph_title
content: From suffix trie to suffix tree

label: text
content: - For each edge we store the offset and length of the corresponding labels

label: text
content: - We additionally store the offset of the full suffixes in the leaves

label: text
content: - Examples:

label: text
content: The longest suffix (top left) has offset zero (and length 12)

label: text
content:
- Top right path: (2,1) => "S"; (3,2) => "SI"; (8,4) => "PPI$"
    Overall offset: 5 (for "SSIPPI$")

label: paragraph_title
content: From suffix trie to suffix tree

label: text
content: - The node label is the concatenated edge labels from the root to the node

label: text
content: Example, leaf 2: (2.1) $> "S"; (3,2)="SI"; $"SSIPPI$"

label: text
content: Thus, the total label for the path to the blue node is: "S" + "S" + "SI" = "SSI"

label: text
content: - As mentioned, the labels are not stored explicitly

label: text
content: They can be directly looked up in the original string (using offset and length)

label: paragraph_title
content: From suffix trie to suffix tree

label: text
content: - Node depth: number of edges from the root to a given node

label: text
content: - Label depth: total length of edge labels (characters) on a path from the root to a given node

label: text
content: - Example for the blue node

label: text
content: Node depth = 2 (two edges)

label: text
content: Label depth = 3 (1 + 2; sum of label lengths along the path)

label: paragraph_title
content: How to build a suffix tree

label: text
content: - Naive method 1: first build a suffix trie and then convert it to a suffix tree by combining non-branching paths and relabeling the edges

label: text
content: - Naive method 2: directly build a suffix tree one suffix at a time (first add entire string, then the suffixes starting at position 1, 2, 3, ...

label: text
content: - These methods take $ \mathcal{O}(m^{2})$ time.

label: text
content: - Is there a difference in the space complexity of the two methods?

label: paragraph_title
content: How to build a suffix tree

label: text
content: One of the most elegant algorithms around is Ukkonen's linear time online suffix tree construction algorithm (Ukkonen, 1995; see also Gusfield's book for a detailed description)

label: text
content: - Memory and time for construction are linear, i.e., $ \mathcal{O}(m) $

label: text
content: - No details here ...

label: text
content: - Basic idea: shorter suffixes are the final parts of longer suffixes, so there is some redundancy in the suffix tree!

label: text
content: Here, for example: the subtree for "NA$" and "NANA$" and "A$" is repeated twice.

label: text
content: - Also the subtree with "$" and "NA$" is used several times, here (see dashed arrows)

label: paragraph_title
content: Suffix tree: find all matches of P in T

label: vision_footnote
content: Walk down path corresponding to P Visit all leaf nodes in subtree (DFS)

label: text
content: - Let $ T $ be our "genome" and $ P $ be a "sequencing read"

label: text
content: - Let k be the number of matches and n be the length of the pattern P

label: text
content: - The search is then $ \mathcal{O}(n+k)$

label: text
content: - Note, the subtree where we stop has $ \mathcal{O}(k)$ nodes and depth first search (DFS) to enumerate these nodes is linear time

label: paragraph_title
content: A note on "generalized" suffix trees

label: text
content: - It may make sense to build a combined suffix tree from more than one input string

label: text
content: For example: the human genome is composed of multiple chromosomes, thus it can be represented by a set of strings" (one per chromosome)!

label: text
content: - Construction:

label: text
content: - Instead of using one termination character, we use $k$ different termination characters, one for each input string!

label: text
content: ★ E.g., "$" for chromosome 1, "#" for chromosome 2,...,"%" for chromosome Y

label: vision_footnote
content: - Example: $ T_{1}=\mathrm{banaanab$

label: paragraph_title
content: - Difference to trees from single strings:

label: text
content: Each leaf is labeled with two integers to identify the input string from which the suffix originates (here illustrated by color instead of an integer), and the position of the suffix within that string

label: text
content: - Also each edge is additionally labeled with an integer to identify the input string

label: text
content: Note: using different terminators ensures that each suffix of each string corresponds to a distinct leaf!

label: paragraph_title
content: A note on "generalized" suffix trees

label: text
content: - Example: $ T_{1}=\mathrm{banana}\$ , $ T_{2} = \mathrm {ananab$

label: text
content: - Pattern matching works as the same way:

label: text
content: - Leaf nodes indicate in which input strings and at what positions a search pattern occurs

label: text
content: - The generalized suffix tree provides the best solution to different problems related to string comparison:

label: text

content: Using a suffix array instead:

label: text
content: - Easy if we have a suffix array of the input string

label: text
content: - Scan through the list to find neighbors with the longest common prefix

label: text
content: While in the original string the occurrences of the longest repeated substring can appear at arbitrary positions, in the suffix array they will always be consecutive (lexicographically sorted)!

label: text
content: Thus: the complexity is $ \mathcal{O}(DN)$ instead of $ \mathcal{O}(DN^2)$

label: paragraph_title
content: How to build a suffix array (Manber and Myers)

label: text
content: - The naive method for constructing the suffix array is not very efficient

label: text
content: - There are linear time construction algorithms (see Shrestha et al., 2014

label: text
content: - We will instead present the simpler $ \mathcal{O}(n\log n)$ algorithm that was described in the paper which first introduced suffix arrays (Manber & Myers, 1990)

label: paragraph_title
content: Manber Myers algorithm

label: text
content: Initialization: sort only the first character of the suffixes (using key-indexed counting sort)

label: text
content: Recursive phase (i): given an array of suffixes sorted on the first $ 2^{i-1}$ characters, create an array of suffixes sorted on the first $ 2^{i}$

label: text
content: Thus: sort 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ... characters

label: text
content: We can perform a single phase in linear time

label: paragraph_title
content: How to build a suffix array (Manber and Myers)

label: text
content: - To sort by 8-mers we can reuse information we have from sorting 4-mers!

label: text
content: - Example: sort the suffixes 0 and 9 ("cacaaaac...$" and "cacaaaaa$")

label: text
content: The first four chars are sorted, se we only need to care about the last four chars

label: text
content: But these last four chars were sorted previously! (They are prefixes of other suffixes!)

label: text
content: To get the index of the second four chars of suffix 0, we look at the suffix at 0+4=4 (rank 7 in sorted list); and for suffix 9, we look at rank 5 in sorted list)

label: text
content: Thus, without comparing the last four chars, we know that suffix 9 comes first!
